tagline: Two dead ends became a mountain crossing between Lincoln and Conway.
intro: The Kancamagus Highway climbs through hairpin turns, crosses a mountain pass and descends beside the Swift River toward Conway. This is the Lincoln-to-Conway portion of New Hampshire Route 112. The Federal Highway Administration lists the Kancamagus as a National Scenic Byway, highlighting overlooks, forest ecology and the Russell Colbath Historic Site. Hiking trails and six national forest campgrounds line the route, extending the journey beyond its roadside outlooks. The Forest Service singles out the route’s fall foliage scenery.

The through road opened in August 1959, when two dead-end roads were joined to connect Lincoln and Conway. Pavement followed in 1964, and the first winter plowing came in 1966–67. The highway bears the name of Kancamagus, the last leader of the Penacook Confederacy.

Travel east from Lincoln beside the East Branch of the Pemigewasset River, then the Hancock Branch, before climbing the hairpins to Kancamagus Pass. On the descent, the Swift River leads into the broad Albany Intervale, then a narrow gorge and two sets of small waterfalls. Along the eastern stretch, the Russell-Colbath House records nineteenth-century settlement, and Albany’s covered bridge spans the river. The highway leaves the national forest and ends at Main Street in Conway, west of downtown.

moments.title: Kancamagus Pass
moments.text: The climb from Lincoln reaches its turning point at Kancamagus Pass: beyond the hairpins, the highway starts descending along the Swift River. There is a scenic outlook near the crest. The river below the eastern side rises here and flows toward the Saco at Conway. On the western approach, the East Branch of the Pemigewasset belongs to a different river system, the Merrimack watershed. The tourism guide identifies nearby outlooks toward the Pemigewasset, the Osceola Range and Mount Hancock. The road follows the Swift River for the remaining 21 miles toward Conway.

moments.title: Passaconaway
moments.text: A central chimney, clapboard walls and a symmetrical front mark the Russell-Colbath House beside the highway. At the front door, sidelight windows and pilasters frame the entrance beneath a simple peaked top. Thomas and Amzi Russell built the house in 1831–32. They operated a sawmill on Oliverian Brook and belonged to a farming and logging community in the valley. Russell descendants owned the house until 1930; it later served as a summer residence before the Forest Service acquired it in 1961. The tourism association identifies it as the area’s only remaining nineteenth-century homestead.
moments.notice: The house has clapboard siding, a central chimney and sidelight windows flanking its entrance.

moments.title: Albany Covered Bridge
moments.text: The covered bridge at Albany spans 120 feet across the Swift River just north of the Kancamagus Highway. The White Mountains tourism guide places a campground beside it and notes displays explaining covered-bridge construction. The Swift continues east through Albany to meet the Saco River at Conway.
moments.notice: The covered span crosses the Swift River just north of the highway.
